cards.front: What is the Drugs and Therapeutics Committee (DTC) of a hospital, and who is suited to convene it?
cards.back: A hospital committee (called the Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee in US usage) that lays down policies and procedures for pharmacy services and medicine use, including the required content of chart orders. A clinical pharmacologist is expected to act as its convener.

cards.front: How does a pharmacopoeia differ from a formulary? Give the Indian examples.
cards.back: A pharmacopoeia (e.g. Indian Pharmacopoeia, IP; also BP, USP) is an official code that sets standards for drug preparations: physical properties and tests for identity, purity and potency. It has legal standing. A formulary (e.g. National Formulary of India) is not a regulatory document; it gives information on available drugs and guides prescribers.

cards.front: Which criteria does the National Formulary of India 2011 use to include a drug?
cards.back: Drugs in the National List of Essential Medicines 2011; drugs used in National Health Programmes; drugs in the Indian Pharmacopoeia; drugs an expert panel recommends though not otherwise covered; any drug the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission finds appropriate.
refs: WEB NHSRC National Formulary of India (NFI) 2011 https://qps.nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-01/National%20Formulary%20of%20India%20(NFI),%202011.pdf

cards.front: What must be weighed when choosing a medicine for a formulary from its therapeutic group?
cards.back: Benefit, risk and cost: efficacy for the indication, safety (fewest adverse effects), and cost judged over the whole treatment course, not only the unit price.
refs: WEB NHSRC National Formulary of India (NFI) 2011 https://qps.nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-01/National%20Formulary%20of%20India%20(NFI),%202011.pdf

cards.front: Is the National Formulary of India a regulatory document?
cards.back: No. It is a guidance document; physicians are expected to use professional judgement, and its drugs were chosen for rational and economic prescribing.
refs: WEB NHSRC National Formulary of India (NFI) 2011 https://qps.nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-01/National%20Formulary%20of%20India%20(NFI),%202011.pdf

cards.front: How does a restricted formulary help a hospital or health system?
cards.back: Keeping a limited list of medicines on the formulary, in standard concentrations, is one of the selection and procurement steps recommended to reduce medication errors. In managed-care settings, formulary controls steer prescribing toward cheaper or preferred generic drugs: the prescriber often picks the drug group and the pharmacist dispenses the single formulary member of that group. The listed drugs may change as prices and rebates are renegotiated.

cards.front: Distinguish generic substitution from therapeutic substitution.
cards.back: Generic substitution: the pharmacist dispenses the cheapest generically equivalent product of the same drug, which many payers require unless the prescriber writes "dispense as written". Therapeutic substitution: dispensing a different drug of the same class; private pharmacists may not do this without the prescriber's permission, though managed-care organisations may follow other policies.

cards.front: Complete: formulary committee measures against prescribing error
cards.text: Pharmacy and Therapeutics committees have added safeguards such as a {{High-Alert Medication}} list (from ISMP) and the use of a {{comma}} when a dose exceeds 999; a hospital order that gives no duration runs until the prescriber stops it or a {{stop-order}} policy ends it.

cards.front: How can a hospital use pharmacoeconomic analysis when it prepares its formulary?
cards.back: It can apply pharmacoeconomic methods (cost-minimisation, cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit and cost-utility) to compare treatments when preparing its formulary of essential medicines. The same analysis helps decide and fix the prices of old and new drugs and supports reimbursement.

cards.front: Define drug information and a drug information centre (DIC). How does a drug information service (DIS) differ?
cards.back: Drug information is written or verbal information on the safe and effective use of therapeutic and diagnostic drugs, given in response to requests from health professionals, committees, patients or the public. PAHO describes a DIC as an operational unit giving objective, timely technical and scientific information on drugs. A DIS is part of a health institution's pharmaceutical services and answers only within that institution. WHO treats independent DICs as a core part of national programmes for rational drug use.

cards.front: Short note: Objectives of a drug information centre

points: Keep an organised database on medicines and therapeutics for practitioners
Give accurate, unbiased medicines information to pharmacists, doctors and other professionals in hospital and community
Train pharmacy students as future medicines-information providers
Promote patient care through rational use of medicines

cards.front: Classify: types of drug information centre
cards.text: {{Hospital-based}} DICs answer in-house queries, help formulary decisions and the P&T committee, coordinate ADR reporting and monitor investigational drugs; {{industry-based}} DICs hold all data on their own products from early development, including unpublished documents; {{community-based}} DICs inform the public about drugs used in national programmes and build awareness.

cards.front: Where and when did drug information centres begin globally and in India?
cards.back: The first DIC opened in 1962 at the University of Kentucky Medical Centre. In India, the Karnataka State Pharmacy Council set up the first independent DIC in August 1997 (registered with IRDIS). WHO India, with the KSPC, then supported five more centres: Sirsa (Haryana), Raipur, Jaipur, Dibrugarh and Panaji.

cards.front: Short note: Functions of a drug information centre

points: Answer enquiries on therapeutic drug use (mainly from professionals, sometimes the public)
Drug evaluation: critical appraisal of published research
Therapeutic advice: efficacy, dose, interactions, adverse effects, administration, adherence
Pharmaceutical advice: availability, formulation, cost, storage, stability
Education and training on rational prescribing
Research, e.g. drug utilisation studies
Pharmacovigilance: enquiries can lead to ADR reports
Toxicology: advice on diagnosis and treatment of poisoning

cards.front: What resources does a drug information centre need, and how is its independence protected?
cards.back: Adequate staff for peak demand, a manager (recruitment, training, promotion, resources, data, quality, liaison), its own library plus electronic databases, basic facilities (phones, internet, computers with backup, photocopier), and specifically trained staff (communication, literature searching, critical analysis, writing, summarising conflicting data). Funding should be independent and stable; external money is accepted only if neutrality is guaranteed, and the service to enquirers should be free.

cards.front: How is quality assured in a drug information centre?
cards.back: By assessing staff, regularly reviewing calls and answers, periodically reviewing resources and procedures, peer review of a random sample of enquiries (ideally with an external drug-information pharmacist or clinical pharmacologist), and feedback from enquirers. Networking between centres allows shared resources, common SOPs, external quality review and inter-site training.

cards.front: Define a medication error.
cards.back: Any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the health professional, patient or consumer (NCC MERP definition). It may arise in prescribing, order communication, labelling, packaging, naming, compounding, dispensing, distribution, administration, education, monitoring or use. Most are latent errors, "accidents waiting to happen", whose causes can be found and fixed.

cards.front: Short note: Types of medication errors

points: Wrong dose, quantity or indication; contraindicated drug
Incomplete history (allergies, other drugs, labs); wrong diagnosis; outdated information
Dose miscalculation; illegible writing; look-alike or sound-alike names; misplaced zeros and decimals; abbreviations; verbal or phone orders
Commission: wrong drug, strength or dosage form
Omission: required drug or dose missed
Contributors: workload, interruptions, no double check, similar names
Omission is commonest
Commission: wrong technique, wrong or expired preparation
Examples: not shaking a suspension, crushing a "do not crush" tablet, swallowing a sublingual tablet, ignoring food instructions

cards.front: Complete: the "five rights" of drug administration
cards.text: Give the right {{dose}} of the right {{drug}} to the right {{patient}} at the right {{time}} by the right {{route}}.

cards.front: How common are medication errors compared with adverse drug events, and what approach reduces them?
cards.back: They are estimated to be 50 to 100 times more common than adverse drug events. Reduction needs a system-based approach covering prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering and monitoring, with trained staff and mandatory, redundant checkpoints.

cards.front: How is the medication error rate calculated, and what rate signals a systemic problem?
cards.back: Number of errors observed divided by the opportunities for error (all doses observed being given plus doses ordered but not given), multiplied by 100. A rate of 5% or more indicates a systemic problem in the facility's drug distribution system.

cards.front: Short note: Error-prone ways of writing a prescription and the safe alternatives

points: Always put a zero before a decimal (".1" can be read as 1)
Never add a trailing zero ("1.0 mg" can be read as 10 mg)
Do not use a slash for a decimal point
Write "units" in full ("10 U" read as 100)
Write "microgram" in full (abbreviation misread as mg: 1000-fold error)
Order the total dose, not "one ampule", when several strengths exist
"QD" is misread as QID
"OD" should mean only right eye
Do not abbreviate drug names (e.g. AZT misread as azathioprine or aztreonam)
e.g. methotrexate and metolazone, apixaban and aripiprazole
Write the indication on the prescription

cards.front: Give examples of errors of omission in hospital chart orders.
cards.back: Vague orders such as "resume pre-op meds" (assumes an accurate list exists), "continue present IV fluids" (no fluid, volume or rate) or "continue eye drops" (no eye, drug, strength or frequency); failing to stop a previous drug when a new one starts; not stating regular versus long-acting form or strength; and "as needed" orders that do not say what condition justifies a dose.

Check patient identity
Independent check of dose calculations

Barcode-assisted administration; standard IV concentrations

Error reporting, root cause analysis, quality improvement

cards.front: Define polypharmacy and distinguish appropriate from inappropriate polypharmacy.
cards.back: Concurrent use of many medicines, commonly taken as five or more (some say six or more) a day. Appropriate: every drug serves an agreed therapeutic goal that is being or can be met, ADR risk is minimised and the patient is willing and able to take them. Inappropriate: one or more drugs are not or no longer needed because there is no evidence-based indication, the goal is not met, the drugs cause or risk ADRs, or the patient cannot or will not take them.

cards.front: What is a prescribing cascade?
cards.back: A cause of polypharmacy in which an adverse drug reaction is misread as a new illness and treated with another drug, exposing the patient to further adverse effects from an unnecessary medicine. Other causes include multiple diseases, multiple prescribers, transitions of care, poor diagnostic skill and self-medication with OTC products and supplements.

cards.front: Define deprescribing and list its steps.
cards.back: The systematic identification and withdrawal of drugs whose actual or potential harm outweighs benefit for that patient's goals, function, life expectancy, values and preferences. Steps: full medication reconciliation; estimate overall risk of drug harm; check each drug for eligibility to stop; prioritise; carry out the withdrawal plan and monitor for withdrawal effects. Tools include Medstopper and deprescribing.org guidelines.

cards.front: Complete: what counts as polypharmacy
cards.text: Polypharmacy is commonly taken as {{five}} or more medicines a day; it is {{appropriate}} when every drug serves an agreed goal, and a {{prescribing cascade}} arises when an ADR is mistaken for a new illness and treated with another drug.

cards.front: Classify: tools to detect inappropriate prescribing in older patients
cards.text: {{Beers}} criteria list potentially inappropriate medicines in older persons by body system; {{STOPP}} screens older persons' prescriptions for inappropriate drugs; {{START}} alerts doctors to the right treatment that is missing; the {{Medication Appropriateness Index}} checks indication, effectiveness, dose, cost and duplication; {{anticholinergic burden}} scales add up anticholinergic load; {{ARMOR}} is a stepwise Assess-Review-Minimize-Optimize-Reassess approach.

cards.front: Complete: SAIL and TIDE techniques to reduce polypharmacy
cards.text: SAIL: keep the regimen {{Simple}}, know the {{Adverse effects}}, give every drug an {{Indication}}, and keep a shared {{List}}. TIDE: give enough {{Time}}, {{Individualise}} doses ("start low, go slow"), avoid {{Drug-drug and drug-disease interactions}}, and {{Educate}} patient and carer.

cards.front: What is medication reconciliation, when is it done, and how?
cards.back: Comparing the patient's new medication orders with everything the patient has been taking, to catch omissions, duplications, dosing errors and interactions. It is done at every transition of care (admission, transfer, discharge, change of prescriber) and at office visits. Steps: obtain the best possible medication history (e.g. "brown bag" review of all medicines brought in, confirmed with carers), list intended prescriptions, compare the two lists, decide on changes, and communicate the new regimen with counselling.

cards.front: What are the goals of a hospital antimicrobial stewardship programme (ASP)?
cards.back: ASPs are ongoing institutional efforts to optimise antimicrobial use in inpatients. Goals: achieve clinical cure while limiting toxicity and resistance by avoiding misuse and overuse; choose the right drug, dose, duration and route, and de-escalate in time; and cut costs without lowering quality of care. Appropriate prescribing and education of patients and doctors achieve these goals.

cards.front: What is the pharmacologist's role in antibiotic policy?
cards.back: The pharmacologist is a core member in formulating national drug policy and the hospital antibiotic policy; in hospitals the clinical pharmacologist drafts the antibiotic policy together with the clinical microbiologist and the head of critical care medicine.

cards.front: What is an antibiotic "time out" and why is it done at 48 hours?
cards.back: A planned reassessment of the need for and choice of an antibiotic about 48 hours after it was started. By then culture and clinical data are clearer, so therapy can be narrowed, switched to oral, or stopped, which limits toxicity and resistance.

cards.front: Short note: Stewardship team and implementation

Clinical microbiologist

Infection control professional
Hospital epidemiologist
IT specialist
Reassess need and choice 48 hours after starting, when clinical and laboratory data are clearer
Dose optimisation; IV-to-oral switch
Adjust for renal or hepatic disease
Avoid interactions and overlapping spectra
Focus on community-acquired pneumonia, UTI, skin and soft-tissue infection
Confirm diagnosis, use culture results, avoid broad spectrum, optimise duration

cards.front: On what does the empirical antibiotic choice for adult hospital-acquired infection depend, according to Katzung?
cards.back: The local antibiogram and the severity of illness.

cards.front: What is a prescription (drug) audit and what does it aim to achieve?
cards.back: A regular review of physicians' prescriptions, typically led by a pharmacologist, to check that therapy is safe, effective and affordable and that hospital practice is evidence-based. It aims to reduce polypharmacy, medication errors and cost to the patient. WHO includes supervision, audit and feedback among its key interventions for rational drug use.

cards.front: Define compliance (adherence) and give the four types of noncompliance.
cards.back: The extent to which patients follow treatment instructions. Noncompliance: (1) the prescription is never obtained (about one-third of patients in some studies); (2) the drug is taken wrongly (dose, frequency, timing, route, duplication, wrong purpose); (3) the drug is stopped early, e.g. when symptoms improve or the bottle is empty; (4) the drug is taken inappropriately, e.g. shared with others.

cards.front: Which four WHO core prescribing indicators does a prescription audit measure?
cards.back: Average number of drugs per encounter; percentage of drugs prescribed by generic name; percentage of encounters with antibiotic or injection use; percentage of drugs from the essential medicines list.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Rational Prescribing Under Pressure: A World Health Organization Indicator and National Medical Commission Compliance Audit With Shift-Based Analysis of Emergency Prescriptions at a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India Cureus 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13312064

cards.front: What is the audit cycle, and why must it be closed?
cards.back: Set a standard, measure current prescribing against it, give feedback and make changes, then re-audit. The cycle is closed only when re-audit shows whether practice actually improved; an audit without feedback and re-audit changes nothing.

cards.front: Short note: Method of a prescription audit

points: State the aim and the drugs or wards to be audited
Choose the standard: standard treatment guidelines, hospital formulary, WHO prescribing indicators, NMC prescription format
Set the criteria and the target level of compliance
Obtain institutional ethics approval; keep patient and prescriber data confidential
Retrospective: prescriptions or case records from a past period
Prospective: prescriptions collected as they are written (OPD, pharmacy, ward)

Standard proforma for every prescription

cards.front: Compare retrospective and prospective prescription audit.
cards.back: Retrospective audit reviews prescriptions or case records already written in a past period; it is quick and cheap, and prescribers cannot change their behaviour, but records may be incomplete. Prospective audit collects prescriptions as they are written; data are more complete and errors can be corrected before harm, but prescribers who know they are watched may change their practice.

cards.front: What are real-world data in drug-safety studies?
cards.back: Routinely collected clinical or insurance records that hold drug exposures, medical encounters and patient comorbidities. Observational pharmacoepidemiology uses them; they are much less cumbersome than trials but still slow and costly to analyse.

cards.front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
cards.back: A partnership between the FDA and more than 30 organisations, including academic sites and managed-care organisations, with curated electronic health data on over 100 million people. Each site analyses data behind its own firewall and returns results, using a common data model.

cards.front: What is an antibiotic 'time-out' in an antimicrobial stewardship programme?
cards.back: A planned reassessment about 48 hours after starting an antibiotic, when the picture is clearer, of whether it is still needed and whether the choice is right.

cards.front: Which colour bag takes sharps such as needles, glass syringes and blades?
cards.back: Blue bag, for sharp objects that can carry infection.

cards.front: Which colour bag takes cytotoxic drug waste?
cards.back: Violet bag: cytotoxic drugs and related waste, contaminated sharps, contaminated animal carcasses and cage linings.

cards.front: Why is a chromate solution prohibited for cleaning lab glassware?
cards.back: Chromates are extremely toxic, including carcinogenic, so their use for cleaning glassware is banned.

cards.front: What is an R-factor, and how does it spread resistance?
cards.back: A plasmid carrying resistance genes. It passes between bacteria mainly by conjugation through a sex pilus; transduction (via bacteriophage) and transformation (uptake of released DNA) also spread it.

cards.front: Are compliance and adherence the same term?
cards.back: The owner books use them as near-synonyms. GG12 lists compliance, adherence, therapeutic alliance and concordance together and says the collaborative doctor-patient relationship matters whichever word is used. Bennett keeps compliance because it also covers doctors who do not follow instructions, and notes that some prefer adherence or concordance, the latter reflecting prescribing by the doctor and taking by the patient.

cards.front: What does GG12 mean by concordance or therapeutic alliance?
cards.back: A collaborative relationship in which doctor and patient each bring expertise: the doctor is the medical expert and the patient is the expert on his own beliefs. The prescriber negotiates and asks whether the patient intends to follow the plan.

cards.front: Which matters more for compliance: actual or perceived disease severity?
cards.back: Perceived severity. Patients comply more when they feel susceptible to the disease, see it as serious, believe the therapy works, judge benefit to outweigh cost, and believe they can carry out the treatment. Actual severity does not predict compliance.

cards.front: Why does the pharmacist matter for patient compliance?
cards.back: Pharmacists often see the patient more often than the physician. Asking about therapy lets them spot noncompliance, educate the patient and inform the prescriber. GG12 cites the Asheville Project as showing better compliance, outcomes and cost with pharmacist-led medication management.

No owner book gives a strict definitional line between the terms
Intentional or accidental errors in dosage or schedule

cards.front: A patient misses the morning dose of a once-daily drug on workdays. What is the likely problem and fix?
cards.back: Dosage or schedule error (timing). Fix: link the dose to a fixed daily cue, such as the coffee-cup cabinet or a meal, and tailor the schedule to the patient lifestyle. GG12 gives a morning-only drug for a night-shift worker as an example of a regimen that does not fit the patient.

cards.front: Why are elderly patients at risk of noncompliance, and is age alone the cause?
cards.back: Barriers include forgetfulness, altered drug handling, less social and financial support, poorer dexterity or senses, and more concurrent medicines. But GG12 states elderly patients are not generally less compliant than other age groups, so the barriers, not age itself, drive the risk.

cards.front: Short note: Types of hospital formulary

points: A formulary is a list of medicine formulations, with varying amounts of added information.
It may list every nationally licensed medicine that health professionals can prescribe.
Or it may list only preferred drugs.
What a third-party payer will reimburse.
The range stocked in one hospital, chosen by its local drugs and therapeutics committee.
A range agreed by a partnership of general practitioners or a primary-care health centre.
Restricted lists aim to contain cost without impairing appropriate prescribing.

cards.front: What is an 'escape clause' in a restricted formulary, and why is it needed?
cards.back: A provision that lets a prescriber obtain a medicine outside the restricted list when a patient has a special need. Without it, a cost-driven list could deny appropriate treatment.

cards.front: Which group chooses the medicines on a hospital formulary?
cards.back: The local drugs and therapeutics committee. Every hospital or group of hospitals should have one, and its restricted list exists to keep costs down without impairing appropriate prescribing.

cards.front: How does computerised prescribing help a prescriber stay within the formulary and prescribe safely?
cards.back: It prompts regular review of the patient's medication list, converts a brand name to its generic name, and gives ready access to formularies and prescribing guidelines.

cards.front: What proportion of family-practice prescriptions are repeats, and what safety concern follows?
cards.back: About two-thirds. Half are issued by the doctor at a consultation and half by the practice nurse or receptionist without the patient seeing the doctor; 95% of requests are granted without further discussion, 25% of repeat patients have had 40 or more repeats, and 55% of patients older than 75 are on repeat medication. The concern is continuing a medicine without periodic review.

cards.front: Why can under-prescribing be as harmful as over-prescribing?
cards.back: Withholding effective treatment harms health. Reasons include lack of information or lack of will to use it, fear of blame for adverse reactions, and fear of sanctions against costly prescribing. Older doctors prescribe less often and at lower cost, but there is no evidence that their patients are worse off.

cards.front: Short note: Primary, secondary and tertiary sources of drug information

points: Original research in journals.
Reports of clinical drug trials and pharmacological research.
They provide the basic factual data.
Derived from primary sources.
Review articles, meta-analyses and compilations of published work.
Bibliographic, abstracting or indexing services: Medline, Current Contents, International Pharmaceutical Abstracts, Index Medicus, Excerpta Medica.
Documents written by individuals or groups, often peer reviewed.
Formularies, standard treatment guidelines, textbooks, general reference books and drug bulletins.
The WHO Model List of Essential Drugs and drug compendia.

cards.front: Essay: Sources of drug information and how to use them

points: Rational drug selection needs comprehensive, objective information.
Sources are grouped as primary, secondary and tertiary.
Original journal research, clinical trial reports and pharmacological research.
Most current and detailed, but not synthesised.
Reviews, meta-analyses and compilations derived from primary work.
Indexing and abstracting services such as Medline, Index Medicus and Excerpta Medica.
Textbooks, formularies, standard treatment guidelines, drug bulletins and compendia.
Often peer reviewed and convenient for practice.
Official compendia are the pharmacopoeia and drug formulary, recognised as legal standards.
Non-official compendia are textbooks, journals and periodicals.
Medline is an electronic database of biomedical literature.
Match the source to the question asked.
Prefer current, unbiased, evidence-based sources.
A drug information centre can appraise and summarise conflicting data.

cards.front: What is a drug compendium, and what are its three groups?
cards.back: A book that is a source of drug information. The groups are official compendia (pharmacopoeia and drug formulary), non-official compendia (textbooks, journals and periodicals), and Medline, an electronic biomedical database. Official compendia are recognised by the government as legal standards.

cards.front: What is the British Pharmaceutical Codex, and what gap does it fill?
cards.back: Published by the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain. It describes drugs, other pharmaceutical substances and formulated products, and provides identity and purity standards for materials for which the British Pharmacopoeia has none.

cards.front: What does Martindale The Complete Drug Reference cover?
cards.back: A compendium published for over 120 years by the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain. It gives unbiased information on medicines used worldwide, including trade names and manufacturer contacts, and also covers plant drugs, diagnostic agents, radiopharmaceuticals, excipients, toxins and poisons. It summarises disease treatments and supports its information with references, systematic reviews, meta-analyses or evidence-based guidelines.

cards.front: Which references give brand-level information on formulations, strengths, cost, dose, precautions, adverse effects and contraindications?
cards.back: Physicians Desk Reference (PDR), Indian Drug Review (IDR), Monthly Index of Medical Specialities (MIMS) and the CIMS India website.

cards.front: What is clinical pharmacy, and what does the clinical pharmacist do?
cards.back: The science of drug formulations, their stability, shelf life and handling. It also covers educating the patient about adherence, counselling on how to take medicines, and monitoring drug therapy for errors. The clinical pharmacist works with the physician to optimise patient care.

cards.front: In one survey of adverse drug events, how severe were they and how many were preventable?
cards.back: 1% were fatal, 12% life-threatening, 30% serious and 57% significant. About half of the life-threatening and serious events were preventable. Among the life-threatening and serious events, prescribing accounted for one-half and administration for one-quarter.

cards.front: What administration error rates are reported in hospital studies, and when do they rise?
cards.back: 15-25%. Rates rise rapidly once four or more drugs are given together. Hospital inpatients receive about six drugs on average, and up to 20 during a stay is not rare.

cards.front: Which simple intervention reduced inappropriate antimicrobial prescribing in hospital studies?
cards.back: Merely supplying information did not change prescribing. Gently asking physicians to justify each prescription produced a marked fall in inappropriate prescribing.

cards.front: Explain the 'Swiss cheese' model of medication error.
cards.back: Each safeguard in the medication-use system is a slice with holes. A single error is usually caught by another check. An adverse event occurs only when holes in several safeguards line up and the error passes through all of them.

cards.front: Distinguish passive from active prevention of medication error.
cards.back: Passive prevention needs no change in the person's behaviour and is the most effective, for example child-resistant packaging, fewer tablets per bottle, or removing a harmful ingredient. Active prevention needs sustained behaviour change by the individual.

cards.front: What is underdosing, and which drugs are most often underdosed?
cards.back: Giving less than the optimal dose in serious illness to avoid adverse effects, which sacrifices efficacy. It is commonest with drugs of low therapeutic index, where effective and toxic dose ranges are close or overlap, such as heparin, anticancer drugs and aminoglycosides.

cards.front: How is polypharmacy defined in Harrison, and how common is it in older Americans?
cards.back: Prescription of multiple medicines, with thresholds generally from five to nine simultaneous drugs. About 40% of Americans aged 65 or older take five to nine medicines, and close to 20% take 10 or more.

cards.front: Why is polypharmacy becoming more common?
cards.back: Rising multimorbidity, a large number of condition-specific guidelines, more medicines that can treat common geriatric conditions, and growing patient and family demand partly driven by television advertising and internet information.

cards.front: How many hospital admissions do adverse drug events cause each year, and which drugs are the main culprits?
cards.back: More than 100,000 per year. The main culprits are warfarin and other antiplatelet agents, and insulin and other hypoglycaemic agents. Cardiovascular drugs (electrolyte and volume disturbance, hypotension, falls, syncope), central nervous system drugs (altered mental status, falls) and antimicrobials are also involved.

cards.front: Short note: General recommendations for prescribing in older patients

points: Evaluate all conditions that could benefit from, be harmed by, or alter the response to drug treatment.
Manage without drugs as often as possible.
Know the pharmacology of the drug and how renal function and hydration affect it.
Avoid serious drug-drug interactions.
For renally cleared drugs, estimate creatinine clearance with Cockcroft-Gault and adjust the dose.
Start with smaller doses and increase gradually until effective or intolerable.
Use blood concentrations to monitor potentially toxic drugs.
Simplify the regimen and use the same dosing schedule for all drugs when feasible.
Time doses with the daily routine.
Account for cognitive impairment, poor hearing and poor vision.
Involve relatives, caregivers and pharmacists.
Check that the patient can reach a pharmacist, afford the medicines and open the container.
Use pillboxes and drug calendars.
Reconcile medicines and educate the patient and family at every hospital discharge.
Keep an updated medication record and review it at each visit.
Monitor adherence, effectiveness and adverse effects regularly.

cards.front: What is the Cockcroft-Gault equation, and why is it used in older patients?
cards.back: Estimated creatinine clearance = (140 - age) x body weight in kg / (72 x serum creatinine), multiplied by 0.85 for women. It tends to underestimate creatinine clearance, which probably makes it the safer formula for adjusting renally cleared drugs in older patients.

cards.front: Short note: Commonly prescribed drugs to consider for deprescribing

points: Diuretics and hypotensive agents when systolic or postural hypotension causes near-syncope or falls.
Antianxiety and hypnotic drugs, especially benzodiazepines.
Psychotropic and other anticholinergic drugs, which cause dry mouth and constipation and raise long-term cognitive risk.
Proton pump inhibitors whose indication is unclear.
Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine after years of use in severe cognitive impairment.
Hypoglycaemic agents in multimorbidity where tight control risks hypoglycaemia.
Statins and prophylactic aspirin in severe chronic illness near the end of life.

cards.front: What are the rates of non-redemption, partial adherence and over-compliance in Bennett?
cards.back: In the UK about 5% of prescriptions are never redeemed, rising to 20% or more in the elderly. Once dispensed, 25-50% of patients take only 50-90% of the prescribed dose or none at all. Up to 20% over-comply, sometimes by 50%.

cards.front: What is antimicrobial stewardship, and what four elements define appropriate therapy?
cards.back: Promoting the choice of the appropriate antimicrobial drug, dosage, route and duration. Programmes use several strategies to improve care through appropriate use, preserve antimicrobials by curbing resistance, reduce adverse effects and control costs.

cards.front: Short note: Three established strategies of an antimicrobial stewardship programme

points: Orders for broad-spectrum or high-cost agents are reviewed regularly by an infectious disease physician or pharmacist.
An alternative is recommended when use can be optimised.
Only a limited set of antimicrobials is included in the hospital formulary.
This limits indiscriminate use and unnecessary expenditure.
Clinicians must obtain approval before using selected antimicrobials.
Approval may be electronic through computerised order entry, after criteria are met, or after discussion with the programme's infectious disease specialist.

cards.front: How does prospective audit and feedback work in an antimicrobial stewardship programme?
cards.back: An infectious disease physician or pharmacist regularly reviews orders for broad-spectrum agents such as carbapenems, or drugs with cheaper alternatives such as daptomycin and ceftazidime-avibactam. When use can be improved, the team recommends an alternative. The approach has reduced broad-spectrum use and Clostridioides difficile infection.

cards.front: Which additional strategies does a stewardship programme use beyond audit, restriction and preauthorization?
cards.back: Guidelines and pathways, dose optimisation, parenteral-to-oral conversion, antibiotic time-out and de-escalation. Teams also encourage documentation of the indication for every antimicrobial and provide ongoing education.

cards.front: What are the CDC's four core elements of outpatient antibiotic stewardship?
cards.back: Ambulatory use accounts for about 85% of antibiotic use in most developed countries. The elements are: commit to improving prescribing; implement at least one policy or practice and assess its effectiveness; monitor prescribing and provide feedback; and provide educational resources to clinicians and patients.

cards.front: Short note: Interventions that reduce inappropriate ambulatory antibiotic prescribing

points: Peer comparison.
Accountable justification.
Precommitment.
Clinical decision support.
Patient education.
Multifaceted interventions.
State a clear diagnosis.
Emphasise positive actions the patient can take.
Review the expected course of the illness.
Name red-flag symptoms that need review.

cards.front: What is an antibiogram, and which one should guide empirical antibiotic therapy?
cards.back: A summary of local antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. The most recent local laboratory antibiogram, updated yearly or half-yearly, is the most useful guide; national resistance rates serve only as a reference. For hospital-acquired infection, the local ICU antibiogram is important.

cards.front: Short note: Requirements of a prescription

points: What is to be given, to whom, and by whom prescribed.
How much, how often, by what route, and for how long or in what total quantity.
Date.
Doctor's address.
Patient's name and address; date of birth is desirable and is legally required for UK children under 12.
Name and dose of the medicine.
Directions to the pharmacist, including total quantity or duration of supply.
Instruction for the patient to be written on the container.
Prescriber's signature.
The format is regulated for precision, safety, efficacy and prevention of fraudulent misuse.
Use only official abbreviations; never invent an abbreviation.

cards.front: What conventions does Bennett give for writing quantities on a prescription?
cards.back: Write 1 g or more in grams; less than 1 g in milligrams (500 mg, not 0.5 g); less than 1 mg in micrograms (100 micrograms, not 0.1 mg). Put a zero before a decimal when no other figure precedes it. Do not abbreviate microgram, nanogram or unit; use millilitre, not cubic centimetre.

cards.front: How is adherence best measured?
cards.back: Directly observed therapy is the most accurate. Finding the drug or its metabolite in plasma is persuasive evidence of recent intake. Tablet counts are weak because a missing tablet need not have been swallowed. Diaries, compartmented boxes, electronic containers that record opening times and physiological markers such as heart rate with a beta-blocker can help.
